title: Chapter 16: Rowboat at Midnight
content: The third stroke is the one that tells her what the water is doing.

Tonight it is doing nothing. Flat and black and easy. The far bank is a smudge with one light on it, and the oars come back heavy, and the boat goes where she puts it, and that is the whole of the job.

Four passengers. A man in a canvas coat with a cooler wedged between his boots. Two women off the cannery line who smell of brine and do not speak. A boy of fourteen who stands up twice and is told twice to sit down.
"Nine," Ade says from the bow.
"Nine what."
"Nine minutes. You are slow."
"I am steady."
"Steady is slow with a good coat on."
He holds the lantern up on a straight arm, and the light falls ahead of them and lies on the water in a long yellow road that is not a road.

Two hundred yards. The current below the landing runs east to west at this hour, so she aims a hundred feet upstream of where she wants to be and lets the river bring her the rest of the way for free.
The west bank comes up out of the dark in pieces. Gravel, ramp, fence.
She does not use the landing. The landing has a chain on it and a sign with an address in Columbus, and she has stopped looking at it.

She puts the bow on the gravel south of the fence, in the shallow where the boat shed ramp runs down, and Ade steps out into six inches of water with the lantern and holds the boat steady while the passengers climb.

The man with the cooler gives her two dollars and does not look at her face. The women give her two dollars each, and one of them says thank you in a voice that has been used all day. The boy stands on the gravel with his hands in his pockets.
"Two dollars," she says.
"I have one."
"Then you have one."
She takes the dollar. He goes up the ramp and stops and turns around.
"Are you the one whose grandfather died."
"Yes."
He thinks about it. "My dad says the gate did it."
"Your dad is right."

Ade drags the bow up and sets the lantern on the post. His jacket is wet to the elbow from holding the boat. He does not say anything about the fence or the sign. He said it all on Thursday, once, and then he stopped.

Thursday is when the county brought the torch. Forty feet of cable went into the water in front of the whole town, and by Friday there was a chain on the landing and a sign with an address four hundred miles away and a man from a security company in Marietta sitting in a truck with the engine running.
By Friday night Wren had the boat in the water.
Second Crossing is fourteen feet of aluminum with three benches, two oars, a bailer, and a patch where Elias put a rivet through it in 2016. It holds four if nobody is large.
On the shed wall, in pencil, in her hand, there are three lines.
FOUR.
NO NIGHT RUNS.
NO WEATHER.

She broke the second one on Friday, because the cannery lets out at eleven twenty and the people who work that line cannot walk nine miles around by the bridge at Mile 14. The clinic is on the west bank. The school is on the west bank. The grocery is on the west bank.
The first line she has not broken.
Not yet.
At nine a man comes down the ramp with a clipboard and stands in the light of the lantern like he is waiting to be photographed.
"Miss Aubrey."
"Pell."
"You cannot run a commercial crossing without a permit."
"Which permit."
"A ferry permit."
"The ferry is condemned." She ships the oars. "This is a rowboat. Four passengers. No schedule. No freight."
"You are charging two dollars."
"Two dollars is not a fare. It is a share of the oars."
Pell writes it down. He is forty and soft through the middle, patient in the way of a man who has been told that patience is a professional skill.
"The county has been notified," he says. "I will be back in the morning with the paper."
"Bring the section number."
"What."
"On the paper. Bring the section number that says a man cannot row his own boat across a river for his neighbors." She picks the oars back up. "I will read it. I read everything now."
Pell stands there. The two women from the cannery are on the bank with their arms folded, watching. Ade is watching with his hands loose at his sides, the way he gets in parking lots.
"Good night, Mr. Pell."
He goes up the ramp.
Ade says, "Share of the oars."
"Shut up."
"That is going in the ledger."

By ten there are thirty people on the west bank. They come down Mill Street past the closed hardware store and stand in a line that runs up the ramp and along the fence, and nobody talks much, and the line does not get shorter, because the boat only holds four.
Ruthie Pyle arrives at ten fifteen with a thermos and a folding chair and sets the chair at the top of the ramp and sits in it like a woman selling tickets.
"Two dollars a head," she says, to the line. "He would have taken a dollar."
"He took nothing," Wren says.
"He took nothing and he knew every name." Ruthie pours into the thermos cup and holds it out. "Drink that. You look like the river."
Mars comes at ten forty with a clipboard and a county jacket and stands at the bottom of the ramp counting heads out loud, because Mars counts things the way other people pray.
At eleven, Vern Ledbetter comes down the ramp on a cane with her granddaughter's hand under her elbow.

She is eighty-eight. She crossed on the ferry on her wedding day in June of 1964, in a white dress, and Elias carried her over the wet boards at the west end so she would not stain the hem, and she has told that story at every funeral in this town for sixty years.
"Mrs. Ledbetter."
"I want a piece of Ruthie's pie," the old woman says. "I have been three weeks without it and I am not going to die without it."
"You could fall."
"I could fall in my own kitchen." She looks at the boat. "My kitchen is bigger than that."
"It is fourteen feet."
"Elias would have had me over by now."
Wren goes up to the shed and gets the book.

It is a hardbound ledger, four hundred pages, and every passenger since 1961 is in it in her grandfather's hand, name and date, one to a line, in ink gone brown at the edges of the older pages. For sixty-five years the book was one hand. Now it is two, and the second one is worse.
The last entry is 12 September. Nine names. The last is Frances Hale, who was on the boat with her daughter and got off alive.
Wren turns the page. She writes the date.
Then, under it, in block letters: SECOND CROSSING.
Then the eight names from the first two trips, in the order they crossed.
Then: Vern Ledbetter. West.
The old woman watches her from the boat, craning.
"Put the dress in," she says.
"What."
"Put it in the book. June the sixth, nineteen sixty-four. So it is written somewhere that I was beautiful."
Wren writes it. Her hand is not steady and the line goes crooked, and she leaves it crooked.
Ade comes up the ramp with the lantern and looks over her shoulder.
"Put me in."
"You are crew."
"Put me in anyway."
She writes: Ade Kessler. East.
He grins like a boy and goes back down to the boat.

Load, push, row, land, unload, count. Her hands blister at the base of the fingers and then the blisters open, and then the tape on the oarlocks goes black and she stops noticing. The river stays flat. The line stays long.
At eleven forty there are eleven people left. She takes four, comes back, takes four, comes back, and there are three left, one of them a woman with a child asleep against her shoulder.
The child is six, maybe. Red boots. A coat with a hood that has gone flat.
"She is out cold," the mother says. "She has been out since seven."
"Put her in the middle."
Ade takes her without being asked, one arm under her knees and one behind her back, and sets her on the middle bench and puts his jacket over her, and the child does not wake up.

The last run leaves the west bank at four minutes past midnight with four aboard. There is no wind. The water is black glass and the oars go in without a sound, and the far bank has one light on it, which is the light on the shed that Ade left on.
Behind her, the fence and the sign and the empty ramp. Ahead of her, the old piling.

She sees it because she always sees it. It is the concrete pier from the original cable landing, 1908, three feet of it above the water at normal flow, with a steel collar around the top where the cable used to run through. At this water it is a foot under, and it makes a small round suck in the current that you can hear if you are listening.
She is listening. She goes wide of it by twenty feet and comes into the gravel below the shed.
The mother carries the child up the ramp. The two men go up after her, and one of them turns at the top and says, "Same time tomorrow?"
"Six," Wren says.
Then the ramp is empty and it is twelve twenty.
Wren sits on the bow with her feet in the water and the book on her knees and does the arithmetic, because arithmetic is what she has.
Ten crossings. Forty fares. Eighty dollars expected, seventy-nine in the coffee can, because the boy had one.
Forty names in the book. Forty-one, counting Ade, who is crew and did not pay and is asleep in the shed with his boots off.
Ruthie comes down the ramp with the empty thermos and stands over her.
"Forty people," Ruthie says.
"Forty-one."
"Forty paid." Ruthie looks at the book. "You wrote all of them down."
"I write all of them down."
"Elias would have counted the money first."
"Elias would have counted the money first."
Ruthie laughs, one short bark. Then she says, "That Pell man will be back."
"He said morning."
"Then go to bed. You have four hours."
Ade sits on the bench with his boots off, winding the lantern cord around his hand and unwinding it. He does that when he wants to say something.
"Say it," she says.
"You could stop. For a week." He does not look up. "Let them drive around by the bridge. You are one woman in a rowboat."
"With a book."
"With a book." He winds the cord. "If you stop, it is not the Authority that closed the river. It is you."
"That is the argument for not stopping."
"That is the argument for sleeping."
There is weather coming. Mars had it on the radio at ten. A front out of the northwest, rain by Thursday, the first cold rain of the year.
Wren looks out at the river. Flat. Black. Doing nothing.
"It will hold," she says.
She sleeps in the chair with the book on her chest and wakes at six with the light in her eyes and her hands too stiff to make a fist.
She walks down the ramp to check the boat.

The security truck is parked at the top of the landing road with its nose against the fence and its engine off. Pell is in the passenger seat with a clipboard on his knees and a thermos between his feet. There is a second man in the driver's seat that she has never seen. He has a camera on a strap around his neck and he is not looking at the river.
He is looking at her.
highlight: Wren rows at midnight, four passengers at a time, until a security truck with a camera parks at the landing.
